title: Andy Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in Labour and among other parties
description: There is renewed attention on the prime minister's push for closer relations with Europe - and that is causing ripples in his own party and others.And
body: There is renewed attention on the prime minister's push for closer relations with Europe - and that is causing ripples in his own party and others.Andy Burnham told his Cabinet earlier this week: "I firmly believe we have ended up with a harder Brexit than people voted for… no sensible person thinks the deal negotiated by the Tories is working for the country."It comes ahead of a week which will focus minds on the UK's relationship with the bloc. On Thursday, at a gathering of European leaders in Dublin, Burnham will for the first time meet those who could prove pivotal as he sells his vision for Britain's future in the bloc.And next week, he will deliver a speech on foreign policy, in which – for Burnham – Europe is a central plank. He will then travel to Brussels for a UK-EU summit to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility.Talking about the new deal to be signed at the summit, Burnham said to ministers: "We will take opportunities that make people in this country better off. "There is a significant prize."This lies behind the prime minister's decision to open the door to the argument about rejoining the EU single market - along with the freedom of movement that would bring - and even the EU altogether.But that longer-term ambition is dividing his cabinet and his party. Some welcome his approach, including those with formerly Brexit-backing constituencies. Angela Rayner, for example, is understood to have been pushing former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer to be bolder on Brexit since at least autumn 2022.The housing secretary is said to have been insistent that Labour needs to stick to its manifesto red lines – not to return to the EU single market, customs union, or freedom of movement – but is open minded to changing those at the next election.Another cabinet minister said: "The best thing you can do in politics is tell the truth. And the truth is that Brexit has been hugely damaging to Britain. "We are not leading a public conversation here, we are racing to catch up with the public."But others are watching nervously at a strategy one former minister described as "high risk".Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, for example, has struck a more cautious tone warning about the "costs and consequences" of rejoining the EU as well as staying out.Jonathan Reynolds, the Business and Trade Secretary, is supportive of getting closer to the EU and discussing the UK's long term relationship. But he has previously warned against joining the EU's customs union and is also unsure about the prospect of rejoining the EU, highlighting the uncertainty of what terms the UK would face, and what the bloc could look like in years to come with nationalist parties in the ascendancy in several European countries.A voice from the past has a different set of concerns. Lord Cameron told Bloomberg's Mishal Husain that starting a conversation about rejoining would be "very long and painful". The former prime minister warned "flirting with rejoining" could also harm Burnham's attempts to renegotiate the Conservative's Brexit deal."If you start endlessly producing this idea that we're actually on a path to rejoining, I think you're in danger of getting a less good partnership deal because of course the EU countries will just think: 'Well, these guys are gonna rejoin anyway, so what's the point in giving them a good partnership deal'."Attitudes in Labour towards the prime minister's approach don't divide along predictable lines. One Scottish Labour MP, personally opposed to Brexit and with a heavily Remain-voting constituency, said it was a "real problem"."How can I argue to my constituents that we had a Scottish referendum in 2014 that settled independence for a generation. but then say the 2016 referendum isn't settled? My view is you accept democracy."For now though, that opposition hasn't broken out into public rebellion, although Labour MP Gareth Snell is one who has warned about reopening the debate.The MP for Stoke-on-Trent, where the Leave vote was 69.4%, told the BBC's Westminster Hour that doing so would "monopolise an awful lot of time inside parliament, inside government" when there are other things MPs should be doing.Two Labour MPs among those most unhappy about Burnham's openness to Europe insisted "there are no plans" for any organised criticism of the prime minister.Despite their concerns, particularly about free movement, they described their current mindset as "wait and see". That temporary truce is likely to fracture if the prime minister's lead in the polls begins to slide.But Burnham's strategy has left other parties struggling to react.The Conservatives have strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules into the future, with the party leader Kemi Badenoch saying that would be a red line and "actually take us backwards".But some Conservative MPs are beginning to express unease about the strategic dilemma presented for their party by Burnham's moves on Europe, fearing that the issue could again divide Conservative voters.In recent months Badenoch and her team have intensified efforts to win back affluent voters, especially in the south of England, who view Burnham's economic offer as too left-wing."The problem is that some of those voters are only just giving us a hearing again after Brexit," one Conservative MP said, "and now they are going to keep being reminded of it."The Liberal Democrats have enjoyed being the most pro-European of the largest parties in Westminster. But some Lib Dems now fear their distinct position risks being drowned out by Burnham.Reform UK though say they are "very bullish" about the return of Brexit to political debate, despite polling that suggests public sentiment has shifted since 2016."If he [Burnham] wants to fight an election on a £40bn bill to rejoin, open door immigration, and less control over our laws and our courts then we are very up for that," a Reform UK strategist said. The party believes that just as it would build a progressive anti-Brexit coalition around Labour, it would also unite Brexit supporters around Reform UK as the most anti-EU party.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in Labour and among other parties

title: Significant drop in levels of toxic 'forever' chemicals in English rivers
description: Levels of the two most toxic "forever" chemicals in England's rivers have dropped by nearly a third over the last decade, according to new figures fro
body: Levels of the two most toxic "forever" chemicals in England's rivers have dropped by nearly a third over the last decade, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA).The decline in the chemicals, PFOS and PFOA, has been put down to stricter restrictions on their use in products after increasing evidence emerged of their damaging impact on human health and the environment.One expert studying the impact of the chemicals said it was "brilliant" to see how far the UK has come on this issue.Thousands of other forever chemicals, known officially as PFAS, remain in use but the regulator said its report showed the need for them all to be better monitored and regulated.PFAS were first developed in the 1930s in the US and became popular with companies making products like frying pans and firefighting foam because of their useful, oil-resistant, water-resistant and electrical properties.They are called forever chemicals because their natural resistance means they take a very long time to break down naturally.The earliest types of these chemicals were called PFOS and PFOA. But two decades ago researchers started to find that they were linked to tissue damage in animals and increased rates of certain serious health conditions such as testicular cancer., external As a result, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010 and PFOA in 2020. The latest data from the regulator, published on Thursday, shows that the concentrations in English rivers of PFOS and PFOA over the last ten years have now fallen by 30% and 29% respectively.Levels in fresh-water fish have fallen 49%. "It's brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years," said Dr David Megson, reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University. There are thought to be around 15,000 other PFAS, although only around 200 are frequently used. The EA said that despite increasing research into these compounds, "uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS". It said its findings "reinforces the need" for regulating all PFAS rather than one by one.The chemicals industry has long opposed such an approach, arguing that there is currently no, or limited, evidence to suggest that other PFAS are toxic and that some have vital uses such as in life-saving medical equipment. The regulator is now regularly testing for 60 other PFAS to build a picture of contamination across the country, and earlier this month the government announced it would begin monitoring levels in people's bodies.The EA report acknowledged that while concentration levels have fallen, because the chemicals take so long to break down, the overall amount still in the environment is likely to have remained unchanged - they have simply been diluted and been washed into the sea."There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused," said Megson.One of the few ways to permanently destroy PFAS is by high-temperature incineration - there are just two such suitable sites in the country currently.

schema.headline: Significant drop in levels of toxic 'forever' chemicals in English rivers

title: Some under-25s should get less benefits, Milburn review to say
description: Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to, under a radical overhaul of the system to be recommended by a government-
body: Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to, under a radical overhaul of the system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.Alan Milburn's year-long report, which will be published on Tuesday, will recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits, the Times reported, external.Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 18- to 24-year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet".He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.His report is expected to recommend that under-25s are no longer able to claim the health element of universal credit or personal independence payment (Pip).Instead, they would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.But many claimants would receive less under the plans, which the government is set to take forward into legislation in the new year.Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.Speaking to the Times about his report, Milburn said: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system."But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances."I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around."Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets, data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year. Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare reform under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.The reforms would represent a radical overhaul of Britain's welfare system, at a time when there is heavy political pressure for the UK to find the money to spend more on defence.If Milburn's recommendations were approved, it could take almost a decade for the British state to see monetary savings.The new system "will need significant investment" and would involve "rebuilding the system from scratch," Milburn added.He said that currently "you've got hundreds of thousands of young people stuck in a benefit system that is trapping them in poverty, giving them no prospect of prosperity or a job".His new proposed system would involve an element of carrot and stick, where young people could lose some of their benefits if they did not engage with the extra work support options."A deal isn't a deal unless there are potential consequences," Milburn said. "Entitlements and responsibilities are two sides of the same coin."A government spokesperson said: "We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work. "But the prime minister has been clear that we need a wholesale change in the way we support young people to grow up in this country, where we invest in their success rather than paying for failure."

schema.headline: Some under-25s should get less benefits, Milburn review to say

title: Police helped remove Russell Brand after 'violent incident' at Jemima Goldsmith's home
description: Police have confirmed they helped Jemima Goldsmith to remove ex-boyfriend Russell Brand from her property in 2014 after she claimed a violent incident
body: Police have confirmed they helped Jemima Goldsmith to remove ex-boyfriend Russell Brand from her property in 2014 after she claimed a violent incident took place.Thames Valley Police said officers were contacted by an alleged victim and went to an address in Oxfordshire on 25 July 2014 but no arrests were made.They listened to her concerns and gave support, and "also ensured the victim's partner left the address, as per the victim's wishes", the police added in a statement on Wednesday.Goldsmith, who dated Brand for about a year, wrote on X on Monday that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.Brand was jailed for 10-and-a-half years for rape and sexual assault on Monday.In her post, 52-year-old Goldsmith, who wasn't part of the trial, said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".She wrote: "I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse."I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident."The Press Association reported that Goldsmith had asked for Brand to leave the property, her wish was then communicated to him by police, and he agreed to leave the house.Goldsmith added: "I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children."I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014. Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."She also said she had "assisted the journalists who finally exposed him", and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" if they were sued.TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.

schema.headline: Police helped remove Russell Brand after 'violent incident' at Jemima Goldsmith's home

title: England v Japan: Eddie Jones sets sights on chaos and upset
description: Japan want 'the sky to fall in' at Twickenham - JonesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Eddie Jones (left) and Steve Borthwick have worked toget
body: Japan want 'the sky to fall in' at Twickenham - JonesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Eddie Jones (left) and Steve Borthwick have worked together with Japan and England in the pastByBBC Sport rugby union news reporterHead coach Eddie Jones says Japan are drawing inspiration from Italy, who beat England for the first time in March, as the Brave Blossoms attempt to heap pressure back on Steve Borthwick with their own landmark win on Saturday.Jones was sacked by England in December 2022 after a miserable autumn which ended in a 27-13 Twickenham defeat by South Africa and jeers from the home fans.The Australian, 66, hopes to cause similar unrest on his return to Allianz Stadium this weekend."We're massive underdogs," Jones told BBC Radio 5 Live."We've got to find a way to disrupt an England side that's looking at New Zealand next week [England play the All Blacks on 21 November] and sometimes may be a little bit distracted."Our opportunity is to get in there, cause some havoc, cause some chaos, put off their game, get the crowd booing. Then the sky starts to come in on Twickenham and you never know what can happen."We've seen it happen with Italy and other countries."Japan have lost all six of their previous Test meetings with England, most recently going down 54-19 on their autumn visit two years ago.However Italy, who won for the first time in 33 attempts earlier this year, and Fiji, who broke their duck with a 30-22 success in 2023, have both secured maiden victories over England during Borthwick's reign.Jones believes England's players are uniquely susceptible to pressure, given a level of scrutiny which is unprecedented in the rest of the global game.Figure caption, Steve Borthwick is 'an outstanding coach': Eddie JonesA run of five successive defeats earlier this year, combined with reports of a rift between players and coaches, raised the stakes for England before Sunday's meeting with Australia.However, Borthwick's players, who had insisted that the squad remains united, delivered an impressive 45-22 victory to vindicate their coach."The noise does get to the team and it can be pretty loud in England," said Jones, for whom Borthwick worked as an assistant during a previous stint with Japan and then with England."You've got a lot of newspapers, a lot of media, probably more than any other country in the world. Sometimes that can weigh down on the players and it's the job of the leadership to get the players thinking straight."Steve's an outstanding coach and a very intelligent man, and a really good coach. So I've got the highest respect for him."Figure caption, England ease pressure on Borthwick after big win over AustraliaEngland back row Henry Pollock scored two tries after replacing the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso on the wing at half-time against Australia, and has been tipped to make only his second start for his country on Saturday.Having also scored a hat-trick off the bench against Fiji in July, Pollock is averaging a try every 22 minutes in the Nations Championship.However, Jones believes the 21-year-old's sky-high strike-rate is not the best measure of him as a player."I wouldn't look too much into it," he said of Pollock's two scores against Australia."Everyone was licking the ice cream on Sunday. They were on the front foot, everyone's lining up to run the ball, there's no pressure in the game."He's a fast back rower, he got the ball in space and he's a talented player, there's no doubt about it, but you couldn't read into it any more than that."Jones is missing his own young star.Fly-half Ryunosuke Ito was plucked from university rugby by Jones, and made his debut against Italy in July without having ever played a professional match.Ito scored his own solo try against Australia in August, neatly stepping through the Wallabies defence., externalImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ito's Test career has been stalled while he completes his obligations to his university teamHowever the 21-year-old fourth-year student, who has established himself as Jones' first-choice fly-half, is required by Meiji University for a collegiate competition, meaning he is missing the northern hemisphere leg of Japan's Nations Championship campaign.Ito will join top-flight Tokyo side Suntory Sungoliath next season, who have former New Zealand captain Sam Cane and Ireland and British and Irish Lions wing James Lowe in their squad."That's the uniqueness of Japanese rugby," added Jones.England v JapanNations ChampionshipSaturday 14 November, 16:40 GMTAllianz Stadium, TwickenhamLive on BBC Radio 5 Live, the BBC Sport website and app

schema.headline: England v Japan: Eddie Jones sets sights on chaos and upset

title: Some Labour MPs speak out against Rosebank as decision looms
description: Some Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments.There is
body: Some Labour MPs have called on the government to reject the Rosebank oil field, saying it is "incompatible" with the UK's climate commitments.There is a growing expectation among senior Labour figures that drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland will be given the go-ahead.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that a decision would be "taken in due course" while Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stressed that affordability of energy bills was her "overriding objective".But in a sign of the division within the party, more than a dozen Labour MPs expressed concerns in Parliament about approving it. Others expressed support, pointing to economic benefits.Supportive Labour MPs said some other parts of the world emitted far more greenhouse gases than the UK and warned of relying on imports. Reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval.Separately, it is understood some Labour backbenchers have organised a letter opposing Rosebank - intended for Burnham, but not yet sent - which more than 60 out of about 400 Labour MPs have indicated they support.One signatory told the BBC that approving Rosebank "would not create new jobs, would bring minimal money into the Treasury and be bad for the climate"."The government's central aim is to tackle the cost of living crisis, and drilling for more oil at Rosebank isn't the answer," the MP said.Wednesday's Westminster Hall - a type of parliamentary debate where backbench MPs raise topical issues but do not vote - was organised by Green MP Carla Denyer.Labour MP for Sheffield Central Abtisam Mohamed told the debate: "Rosebank fails on every test."It will not benefit taxpayers who will shoulder the vast majority of the development costs, it will not strengthen our energy security because most of the oil will be sold on international markets, and it will not reduce energy bills for our constituents, who will remain exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices."Richard Burgon, a former frontbencher on the left of the party, said: "Rosebank is not compatible with our climate targets - it's dangerous to pretend otherwise."The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period.The UK government has always insisted that Rosebank is a quasi-judicial decision, formally resting with Fahnbulleh. She green-lit production in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea last month, but Rosebank hangs in the balance.During the debate, Labour MP Anna Gelderd said: "We live in an unprecedented era where our energy security is more vital than ever, in which jobs and wealth must be protected and economic opportunities seized - on both of these points, Rosebank fails."Labour MP Julia Buckley said she had received opposition to Rosebank from her constituents in "regularly flooded Shrewsbury" and said fossil fuels "belong in the past, not the future".She urged Fahnbulleh to "reject the oil licence in favour of renewables", adding: "Please don't add further to our climate emergency."Other Labour MPs expressed their support, including recently departed veterans minister Al Carns, who warned that Britain would continue to need fossil fuels for decades and importing more would be a mistake."Refusing to produce it here does nothing on its own to eliminate that demand - it simply increases our reliance on imports which can carry their own environmental cost," he added.Those representing communities with ties to the oil and gas industry, including Jonathan Brash, the Labour MP for Hartlepool, stressed the benefits of approving Rosebank for British jobs.Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, Labour MP Bill Esterson, chair of Energy Security and Net Zero Committee, said "the economics of it (Rosebank) are that you should carry on with it" and "there's an element of energy security" by approving it.Energy minister Michael Shanks told the debate the government would take a "pragmatic approach" to a clean energy transition, stressing it was "not a turn off the taps government, but nor can we justifiably be a drill every last drop government either"."This government will not make decisions for this country which are not compatible with our climate obligations," he added.

schema.headline: Some Labour MPs speak out against Rosebank as decision looms

title: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax
description: Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities.In Italy
body: Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities.In Italy a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution but Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger"."These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook. Scotland's education secretary Mairi McAllan said there was no risk to the public and specialist cyber-crime officers were working to identify the source of the messages. In Northern Ireland education officials told schools to remain open unless otherwise advised by police.It is unclear whether the incidents are connected."As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," McAllan said.Scottish police had earlier said that the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes. However some local authorities confirmed that some schools had been evacuated."Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails," Police Scotland said.Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent on Wednesday to the inboxes of 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 state schools, and private schools were unaffected.The message, said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan", caused alarm in many schools.The BBC has seen the email sent to Scottish schools which appeared to have similar wording, and also referenced the name Mikhail Andropov, although as leader of a "Red Owl" project.Italy's Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the incidents involving Italian schools were probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk", adding that there appeared to be a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in across Europe targeting flights, supermarkets and even hospitals.Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption. Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.On Wednesday one Milan headteacher, Anna Bertato, told Italian media she had checked the email address of the sender online: "It was already classified as spam by a student at a university in Taiwan."Another Milan headteacher, Massimo Nunzio Barrella, told Adnkronos news agency that he had immediately realised the email was spam when it arrived in his inbox at 08:59 and he decided not to evacuate his school and reassured parents who phoned in."The text seemed almost comical," said Barrella, "it was like a message from Martians: 'We have come to annihilate you.' I even had a bit of a laugh."Although many schools were initially evacuated on Wednesday, the alarm was quickly lifted, and pupils were allowed to return to class. Some parents decided to take their children home for the day, but the majority of schools in Milan did not send their pupils home.Some 280 school head teachers had already received threats in recent days, according to Italian reports.In a statement, the head of the central Umbria region Stefania Proietti said "checks conducted so far in Umbrian schools have proved negative, and law enforcement is working rapidly and carefully to verify each report".

schema.headline: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax

title: Famed ship SS United States to be sunk off coast of Florida
description: Figure caption, This archival video shows the SS United States in 2025 as it starts its move to Florida on its way to become the world's largest artif
body: Figure caption, This archival video shows the SS United States in 2025 as it starts its move to Florida on its way to become the world's largest artificial reef.ByAna FaguyA ship that was once the fastest in the world and is longer than the Titanic will be sunk off the coast of Florida and turned into the world's largest artificial ocean reef.The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will soon become a home for sealife and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.Instead, after being purchased by a Florida county, it will be added to the dozens of artificial reefs off the coast, as a land-based museum detailing the ship's history is also planned.Image source, Getty ImagesBefore its retirement, the SS United States was known for carrying royalty and celebrities from the US the Europe, beginning in 1952 and ending in 1969. A young Bill Clinton, before he was president, used the ship to cross the Atlantic. Former presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John Kennedy also travelled on the vessel.The ship was moved from Philadelphia to Alabama last year for cleaning and remediation work. On Monday, it took its final journey from Alabama to the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will be sunk on Wednesday in a precision operation without explosives. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A 2015 image from when the ship was docked in PhiladelphiaStars including Marlon Brando, Coco Chanel, Duke Ellington, Salvador Dali, Walt Disney, Judy Garland and Cary Grant also boarded the ship during its sailing lifetime.Before its purchase by the municipal Florida government, a number of proposals that would have seen the ship live a second life as a museum or a floating hotel failed. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, SS United States in the 1950'sInstead, the famed ship sat at various docks with various owners as legal battles played out. The SS United States Conservancy group repeatedly attempted to keep the ship above water, but was unsuccessful.Conservancy President Susan Gibbs - whose grandfather helped design the SS United States - said she was glad that the story of the ship would live on. "[The ship] has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together," Gibbs told CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

schema.headline: Famed ship SS United States to be sunk off coast of Florida

title: Sunbed firms must not downplay cancer risk, says watchdog
description: A watchdog has launched a crackdown on misleading sunbed adverts, warning tanning firms they must not claim their beds are safe or can treat medical c
body: A watchdog has launched a crackdown on misleading sunbed adverts, warning tanning firms they must not claim their beds are safe or can treat medical conditions.The Committee for Advertising Practice (CAP) said it was issuing a UK-wide enforcement notice to "send a clear message to the industry that advertisers must not downplay the risks associated with sunbed use".Earlier this year, the BBC identified hundreds of social media videos claiming the beds could boost energy and treat skin conditions or mental health problems.The Sunbed Association, which represents around half of the UK's tanning salons, said it fully supported action against misleading adverts, but said businesses must still be allowed to demonstrate they operate responsibly.The CAP, which draws up the UK's advertising rules, said some of the claims being made by companies were potentially harmful and could discourage customers from seeking appropriate medical treatment or advice. "Sunbeds carry serious health risks, including an increased risk of skin cancer," said the CAP's compliance executive James Burnett. "Ads shouldn't downplay those risks or present sunbed use as a way to improve health."Cancer charities and doctors are clear about the risks of using sunbeds - and say the machines are linked to higher rates of melanoma and other skin cancers.Using a bed before the age of 35 increases the risk of melanoma by 59% later in life, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).Young people are by far the biggest sunbed users in the UK - about one in seven 18-to-24-year-olds say they used one in the past year, double the average for all age groups, according to a 2025 YouGov survey.Rosie Vare, health information manager at Teenage Cancer Trust, said skin cancer was one of the most common forms of the disease in young adults and she welcomed stricter enforcement of the advertising rules."We want young people to be properly informed about the risk of sunbed use and we recommend using trusted, regulated sources to find out information such as the NHS, external or cancer charities, external," she added.Sunbed use is legal and regulated in all parts of the UK, with limits on the strength of the UV light the beds can emit and a ban on under-18s using the devices.According to the Sunbed Association, its members train staff to screen out high-risk customers with very fair skin and, under its guidelines, no individual should be allowed to buy more than 60 sessions a year.The organisation's chairman, Gary Lipman, said he would never encourage members to use health claims to promote their products. He said he has worked with the CAP to ensure the code would not stop members explaining how they comply with regulations."We fully support action against misleading advertising. But there is a world of difference between claiming something is risk free and explaining that a business operates responsibly," he said.The CAP said that advertisers have been given until 7 December 2026 to make sure any marketing claims are compliant. It said it would be using an AI-based monitoring system to identify ads that continue to break the rules and would "take further action where needed".

schema.headline: Sunbed firms must not downplay cancer risk, says watchdog

title: David Walliams: Author Chloe Combi says there were 'real concerns' about him in publishing industry
description: Combi said she was getting invited to events such as book launches around the time one of her own books was being published, and was also running a sc
body: Combi said she was getting invited to events such as book launches around the time one of her own books was being published, and was also running a scheme to bring "high-profile and inspiring writers and speakers" to talk in schools.At an event in 2015, Combi said she got speaking to someone "quite senior" in publishing, who warned her about Walliams. "We were talking about [the scheme] and possible writers who might be good for the project to work well with teenagers," Combi said."She gave me some great recommendations and said to me: 'Whatever you do, don't invite David Walliams, and FYI if you are speaking to head teachers or teachers, please inform them that he's not a good booking, not an appropriate booking for a school'."Combi continued: "I obviously asked why, and to be honest I had already heard quite a lot of rumours because those worlds are quite small and contained."One of the things she said was that there had been real concerns about his behaviour around young female staff."If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.Asked whether concerns about his behaviour was an open secret, Combi replied: "Yes definitely... and I'd heard it from people who worked in publishing, fellow writers, people kind of in celebrity and TV circles."Combi said she never met Walliams herself, and said her information had come from "a number of people I was speaking to".HarperCollins in September announced it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue. Earlier on Wednesday, media minister Ian Murray said there is a "cultural problem" in the industry that needs to be "stamped out".Giving evidence to the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, Murray said he was "deeply saddened and also angry" to see the prevalence of abuse by men in the media industry.Meanwhile, Minister for Women and Equalities Bridget Phillipson paid tribute to the "bravery" of victims who have shared their experiences in recent days.Speaking in the Commons, she said: "Women and girls should never have to shrink our lives or ambitions because of outdated, misogynistic attitudes, and the appalling testimonies we have heard in recent days underline how much further we have to go."Phillipson later said the government would "go further" on restricting the use of non-disclosure agreements, telling Sky News: "We cannot have a system where rich and powerful individuals, rich and powerful men, are able to silence women, buy their silence and stop things coming to light."She said that she believed injunctions were being misused, and that her colleagues at the Ministry of Justice were looking at how the government can intervene to ensure this did not happen.Comedian and podcaster Deborah Frances-White told BBC Radio 4's The World at One that young women are "definitely" still being exploited in the comedy industry.She told the programme that perpetrators understand consent but they just enjoy the power that comes with ignoring it, adding: "The thrill is in the contravention of consent."Asked whether she recognised the picture Russell Brand's conviction and allegations against Walliams had painted of the comedy industry, she said: "Yes, entirely."She described an industry where she was asked to meet male producers in darkly lit rooms "walking a tightrope", having to make them feel attractive and avoid being assaulted as they influenced future employment opportunities.She said these events are "definitely still going on" and that she is in a WhatsApp group with female comedians who share their experiences with each other.

schema.headline: David Walliams: Author Chloe Combi says there were 'real concerns' about him in publishing industry

title: Scottish man confirmed as victim of Krakow shooting
description: Image source, FacebookImage caption, James Thomas Campbell is understood to have died in the Krakow shootingA 32-year-old Scottish man has been confir
body: Image source, FacebookImage caption, James Thomas Campbell is understood to have died in the Krakow shootingA 32-year-old Scottish man has been confirmed as one of the victims of a mass shooting in Poland that left six people dead.The man, who is understood to be James Thomas Campbell from Prestwick in South Ayrshire, died when a lone gunman opened fire in central Krakow on Saturday.Campbell worked as a DJ in Ayrshire. Police Scotland confirmed it was providing specialist support to the victim's family, but formal identification is yet to be carried out.The 24-year-old attacker, named as Michal Oksinski by local media, died in hospital on Monday, having also fatally shot four Polish citizens and an Austrian woman with a further 15 people, including two police officers, injured.Det Ch Insp David McAlinden, senior investigating officer from Police Scotland's Counter Terrorism Policing unit, said the force was "aware of the tragic death of a Scottish man in Krakow".He added: "Working in conjunction with COPFS (the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service), Police Scotland is supporting the UK counter-terrorism policing network and the Polish authorities. "The immediate shared priority is to ensure that identification is properly established for the family, so that repatriation can take place as quickly as possible."The family has asked for their privacy to be respected. Our thoughts are with them and everyone impacted by this incident."Mark Jewell, a close friend of Campbell's who regularly DJ'd with him, described him as "a quiet, kind and soft-hearted person, who wouldn't have harmed a fly".He added: "It's just so tragic that he had to be in the wrong place at the wrong time."I had been speaking with him when he was headed over to Poland and I messaged him as soon as I heard about the terrible attack, to ask if he was safe - not for one minute expecting that he would have been caught up in it all."I was fully expecting a funny message back from him, saying not to worry. I can't quite get my head round it all."Image caption, The attack happened in Krakow on SaturdayThe attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, a popular tourist spot.Police said the gunman drove into the square before beginning to fire at random people from his car.Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the man, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning.In addition to the six people killed in central Krakow, police later found the bodies of the gunman's parents and sister at his address on Saturday.Earlier this week two friends from Aberdeen described how they ran for their lives as the shooting started.Ciaran McMenemy, 26, and Charlie Hutchison, 27, said they had just sat down for a drink when the gunfire began. They quickly fled and took shelter.

schema.headline: Scottish man confirmed as victim of Krakow shooting

title: Max strength cold and flu pills – are they worth the money?
description: Cold and flu drugs fall into three broad camps: household names such as Lemsip and Sudafed; supermarket own-label alternatives; and single-ingredient
body: Cold and flu drugs fall into three broad camps: household names such as Lemsip and Sudafed; supermarket own-label alternatives; and single-ingredient medicines containing paracetamol or ibuprofen.The difference in price can be striking.A packet of 16 Lemsip All-In-One Max Strength tablets retails at £7.30, more than 20 times the £0.35 cost of paracetamol pills in some supermarkets.Both contain 500mg of paracetamol, which doesn't treat the underlying infection but does relieve pain and can bring down a fever.The Lemsip version, along with many of its competitors, also contains the decongestant phenylephrine.It's meant to constrict leaky or swollen blood vessels in the nose which can cause congestion.But Prof Lawrence says there is little evidence it works when taken as a tablet, rather than as a nasal spray, because much of the drug is broken down before it can reach the bloodstream.In 2024, the US drug regulator said it wanted phenylephrine removed from all cold and flu pills, saying it was simply not effective, although that proposal has yet to be finalised.Some cold and flu remedies contain a third active ingredient - guaifenesin - which is meant to loosen mucus in the airways.That sits in more of a grey area: some studies report improvements in chest congestion, while others find little or no benefit.A spokeswoman for Reckitt, which owns Lemsip and Nurofen, said the ingredients in its products are approved by regulators and formulated for multiple symptoms including fever, congestion and coughs.Yet ingredients are only part of the story.Bigger brands have more money to spend on in-store adverts and displays, according to a former manager at a large chemist chain.Well-known names or premium own-label products are often positioned at eye level, while budget alternatives are tucked away on the bottom shelves."You are always going to promote the ones which are more expensive," says the former manager, who doesn't want to be named as she still works in the industry.When it comes to medicines, some shoppers assume that paying extra means getting something more trusted or effective."Nine times out of ten, people would come in and ask for a certain brand," she adds."Even if I explained there was little difference, and I was only trying to save them money, they would still want the big name."The PAGB, which represents the consumer healthcare sector, argues that "trusted and recognisable" brands can simplify choice and build confidence at a time when "health misinformation is widespread".

schema.headline: Max strength cold and flu pills – are they worth the money?

title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
description: Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.Although the Ame
body: Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon. Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest.""I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible. Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said. After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky. The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member. For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence. Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin. Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them. Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security. Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said.Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again."These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."

schema.headline: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough

title: 'You're triggering me': How to understand your therapy-speak teen
description: Mum-of-four Shannon, from New Jersey, says it took her several years to learn her approach of "I'm your parent and I'm asking you a question and you a
body: Mum-of-four Shannon, from New Jersey, says it took her several years to learn her approach of "I'm your parent and I'm asking you a question and you are going to answer me" was not helpful for her teenagers.She became frustrated when they would push back - sometimes using phrases about her not respecting their boundaries.Samuel says carefully choosing when and how you talk to your teenager can help them talk more openly, instead of hiding behind therapy speak.Rather than asking them in a direct manner, she suggests talking about yourself being in a similar situation."You could bring up a subject about yourself at school or something that's related... so it isn't kind of pointing a finger at them," she says. Shannon says: "I've noticed when I do back off they will then come to me later to say, 'Hey, guess what? I got a 95 on that Spanish test'... You don't have to ask them for three days straight about something."Carla is glad she's open with her teenagers and feels they can discuss things with her - even if she sometimes struggles with the meaning."We are close and I think that's why sometimes they think that they can use these [therapy] words, as if they're talking to a friend."If you or someone you know is experiencing mental or emotional distress, you can access support from the BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: 'You're triggering me': How to understand your therapy-speak teen
